summary: Redwood AE + SE walked Atlas Financial through Redwood Optimize recommendations focused on batching and prefix/KV caching to reduce per-token cost while meeting latency SLOs. Discussed tradeoffs for Hosted vs Dedicated, example cost math for 1M monthly requests, recommended initial config (batch size target, TTLs, cache key strategy), and next steps to run a 2-week benchmark on Dedicated. Action items assigned for sharing spreadsheets, traffic dump, and a proposed pilot schedule.
topics: Prefix / KV cache behavior and hit-rate modeling
transcript:
[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — this is Jordan from Redwood, AE, and today we wanted to run through Optimize specific recommendations around batching and KV/prefix caching. Uh, Priya and Luca are here to cover the config and cost model math.
[00:12] Michael: Great thanks, we've been trying to figure out how to lower token spend without regressing latency for our financial summarization endpoint, so excited to see concrete numbers.
[00:22] Priya: Awesome, quick agenda — 1) understand your traffic shape 2) batching knobs and safe targets 3) prefix/KV cache strategies 4) cost model with sample numbers and tradeoffs, then Q&A.
[00:33] Aisha: Sounds good. For context, our summarize endpoint is about 70% of calls, median request length is ~220 input tokens, response median ~180 tokens, p95 latency target is 300ms, and we run this in us-east.
[00:48] Priya: Good, that helps. Two quick clarifications: are you doing streaming to the client now, and what's your concurrency distribution?
[00:55] Samir: We stream yes, but some clients still poll. Concurrency is bursty — typical steady is 40 c/s, bursts up to 700 c/s during market opens.
[01:06] Priya: Right. So batching helps when you can tolerate micro added latency — we usually see optimal per-token cost improvement at batch sizes between 4 and 16 depending on the model and HW. For low-latency p95 requirements we recommend targeting a median batch size of 4 with opportunistic batching to 8 during higher concurrency.
[01:25] Jordan: To add, Redwood Optimize will suggest batch thresholds by observing your concurrency and arrival distribution; you can set a max latency SLO to cap batch wait.
[01:34] Michael: Can you give a concrete example of the tradeoff? Like how much latency are we adding for these batch sizes and what's the token saving?
[01:42] Priya: Sure. Example (rough numbers): single-shot inference on our 70B quantized variant — per-token compute cost baseline X. If you batch 8 at once you amortize model init and KV cache overheads. In practice we've seen 20-40% token-equivalent cost reduction attributable to batching alone when you go from batch size 1 to 8, but this depends on the model and sequence lengths. Latency-wise, if your arrival rate is low and you hold for 25ms to build a batch you might add ~25-40ms median; if you use a max-wait SLA of 50ms the p95 delta can still be controlled.
[02:20] Aisha: That 20-40% sounds great, when does KV/prefix caching come into play though?
[02:27] Priya: Good question. Two patterns — prefix cache (we cache the KV for identical prefixes, useful for multi-turn/stateful flows) and full KV cache that stores computed KV states keyed by prompt fingerprints for reuse. With prefix hits you avoid re-computing attention states for the prefix tokens and only generate on suffix, which reduces compute proportional to prefix length.
[02:45] Jules: Our use case has a long fixed intro prompt and then a shorter user input — seems prefix caching could be high ROI.
[02:52] Priya: Exactly. If your prefix is 120 tokens and the generated suffix is 80 tokens, a 50% prefix hit rate reduces overall token compute by about 40% for that call.
[03:03] Samir: What's realistic hit-rate? We have personalization tokens in the prompt so exact hits may be lower.
[03:09] Priya: Often you see 10-50% depending on how templated the prompt is. We recommend canonicalizing prompts (remove noisy tokens, use stable IDs) and applying a short TTL on cache keys.
[03:20] Michael: Can you walk through the cost-model spreadsheet?
[03:25] Jordan: Yep — we'll send the raw sheet after the call, but high level: you model baseline token count per request, model throughput cost (per-token compute), and then apply predicted reductions from batching (amortization) and cache hit rates.
[03:38] Priya: Example scenario we discussed live: 1M requests/month, average total tokens per request 400 (input+output). Baseline cost assumption: $0.06 per 1k tokens for the particular model variant (hosted). So baseline monthly cost = (1,000,000 * 400) / 1000 * $0.06 = $24,000.
[03:57] Priya: If you achieve 30% effective token reduction via batching + prefix cache combined, that drops to $16,800 — roughly $7.2k savings monthly. That roughly matches our internal atlas-style example.
[04:14] Aisha: Nice. How does Dedicated pricing change the math?
[04:18] Jordan: Dedicated moves you to committed capacity so you trade unit pricing and utilization. If your 1M requests map to predictable utilization that fills a fraction of a GPU, the effective per-token cost can be lower but you need to account for reserved seat costs. Our recommendation: run a 2-week dedicated benchmark to measure effective tokens/sec and tail latencies under your traffic. We can help size the pool and run the benchmark.
[04:39] Michael: What about KV cache memory pressure — we're using k8s nodes with limited GPU memory.
[04:45] Priya: KV cache is stored on the serving nodes, and memory grows with sequence length and active sessions. We suggest limits: TTL of 5-15 minutes for high-churn workloads, and evict least-recently-used entries. For long-lived sessions (like multi-turn support) you can pin sessions to a node in Dedicated to avoid cold-starts.
[05:06] Samir: Any heuristics for TTL?
[05:09] Priya: If your users have 1-2 interactions per session within 3 minutes, a TTL of 5 minutes captures most hits without high memory growth. If sessions are multi-hour, consider explicit session persist or per-customer mini-pools.
[05:20] Luca: Also note the KV footprint is roughly proportional to prefix token count times active sessions; we usually show a projection in the workbook.
[05:29] Aisha: Let's talk about batching + streaming. We have clients that need incremental tokens to display — does batching break streaming?
[05:36] Priya: Streaming is compatible — Redwood supports partial responses and streaming from inside a batch. We can stream the first token as soon as it's available from the combined batch result. The tradeoff is slightly more complex coordination but it's supported. Some early transcripts from our infra show minor jitter but overall clients accepted it.
[05:53] Michael: Any pitfalls we should watch for during pilot?
[05:58] Jordan: Common pitfalls: 1) naive batching without adaptive wait leads to p95 spikes during low traffic, 2) caching with overly long TTLs causes stale personalization, 3) quantization/model variant mismatch between test and prod leading to quality regressions.
[06:12] Aisha: How do you recommend we measure quality during the experiment?
[06:16] Priya: We recommend a small eval set of prompts and automatic token-level diffs plus sampling-based human review for hallucination/regression. Redwood Optimize can run these evals and tie changes to alerts.
[06:28] Jules: For the benchmark, we can share 48 hours of traces — do you need user ids sanitized?
[06:33] Jordan: Yes, please remove PII and replace user ids with stable hashed ids; that still lets us measure prefix reuse.
[06:40] Michael: About the cost numbers — you used $0.06 per 1k tokens earlier for hosted. Is that negotiable?
[06:45] Jordan: Hosted list varies by model; for larger committed Dedicated contracts we can give lower unit pricing. That's part of the deal conversation. For the cost-model spreadsheet we'll surface a Hosted baseline and a Dedicated committed scenario.
[06:59] Priya: Quick note on quantization: moving from FP16 to 4-bit quant can drop per-token inference cost by ~20-35% dependent on model while sometimes impacting perplexity. That's another knob in the workbook.
[07:10] Samir: How do we validate that the quantized model's outputs are acceptable?
[07:13] Priya: Run paired A/B evals on a held-out sample and monitor quality metrics. Redwood supports automatic regression detection and rolling back to FP16 variants.
[07:26] Michael: Ok, let's go deeper on the caching key strategy.
[07:29] Priya: Primary advice: canonicalize prompt templates, token-normalize fields that are variable (timestamps, IDs), and use a two-tier key: (template-id + hashed canonicalized text). That increases cache hit-rate and avoids accidental collisions.
[07:45] Aisha: Can we have per-tenant cache partitions? We need isolation for compliance.
[07:50] Jordan: Yes — Dedicated supports per-tenant namespaces and RBAC for cache access; for Hosted there's logical namespaces and strict encryption and audit logs. We'll include security docs.
[07:59] Jules: Also curious about autoscaling and how it interacts with cache warm-up.
[08:03] Priya: Autoscaling can cause cache cold starts on new nodes. To mitigate: stagger scale-up with pre-warmed containers, or in Dedicated use pinned nodes for high-heat routes. We can also preload top N prefixes if you share them.
[08:17] Michael: Could you show the sample rows from the cost-model?
[08:20] Priya: Sure i will read a couple lines — baseline: 1M reqs, 400 tokens/req, hosted $0.06 per 1k tokens -> $24k. Scenario A: batching only 20% reduction -> $19.2k. Scenario B: caching only 25% reduction -> $18k. Combined conservative: 35% -> $15.6k. Combined optimistic: 50% -> $12k. These are examples, real world tends to sit in 25-40% for templated workloads.
[08:45] Michael: That matches earlier slide i think. Can we get that sheet?
[08:48] Jordan: Yes will send.
[08:50] [08:50] — brief screen share glitch, audio drop for 6s —
[08:56] Priya: Back on, sorry.
[09:00] Aisha: One more question on instrumentation — what metrics do you collect out-of-box?
[09:04] Luca: Redwood Console provides token breakdown per-route, batch size histograms, cache hit/miss rates, p50/p95/p99 latency, cost per token and per-route cost. You can export time series to your observability stack.
[09:17] Samir: Is there an SDK or tracer we drop in?
[09:20] Jordan: We have a small agent and SDKs (python, go, node) to emit route tags and trace ids.
[09:26] Michael: Ok this is helpful. Let's discuss pilot timeline — we want results before end of quarter.
[09:32] Jordan: Tight but doable. Proposed plan: Week 0 - share prompt set + traces; Week 1 - Redwood runs config simulation and initial Dedicated sizing; Week 2 - 1-week Dedicated benchmark; Week 3 - analyze and recommend final config. We can compress if you want.
[09:48] Aisha: Sounds good. For the Dedicated benchmark, what do you need from us?
[09:52] Priya: The 48h traces sanitized, a list of top 50 prefixes, your p95 SLOs per route, and any compliance constraints for the test environment.
[09:59] Michael: We'll get that to you.
[10:02] Jordan: Great. Quick recap — Jordan will send cost-model workbook and deck; Priya will propose batching + cache config and schedule the benchmark; Atlas to provide traces. Any final questions?
[10:12] Jules: One ask — can you include a tab that models streaming vs non-streaming cost differences?
[10:16] Priya: Yes we'll add streaming delta in the workbook.
[10:19] Michael: Thanks everyone.
[10:21] Jordan: Thanks all, we'll follow up with the spreadsheet and scheduling notes.
[10:25] [End of recording — meeting wraps at 15:46 PDT]
